pronunciation.note: Ise is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. Its significance is cultic and geographic, not orthographic.

domains.title: Sacred City of the Imperial Kami
domains.subtitle: Shrine, Pilgrimage, and the Heart of Shinto
domains.lead: Ise is not merely a place; it is the spiritual center of Shinto and the home of Amaterasu, the sun goddess and ancestor of the imperial house. For more than a thousand years, the Ise Grand Shrine has been rebuilt every twenty years in an unbroken cycle of renewal, making Ise a city where architecture, nature, and divine presence are continuously reborn.

cards.name: Ise Grand Shrine
cards.desc: The most sacred Shinto complex, rebuilt every twenty years in the shikinen-zōtai tradition.

cards.name: Amaterasu's Dwelling
cards.desc: The Inner Shrine houses the mirror, one of the Three Imperial Regalia.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Center
cards.desc: For centuries pilgrims traveled the Ise-kaidō to visit the shrines.

cards.name: Renewal Architecture
cards.desc: The shrines are rebuilt from new cypress in a cycle of death and rebirth.

mythology.lead: Ise's mythology is inseparable from the mythology of Amaterasu and the imperial house. The city exists because the sun goddess needed a dwelling worthy of her.

myths.title: Amaterasu Comes to Ise
myths.text: According to tradition, the imperial princess Yamatohime-no-mikoto traveled for twenty years searching for a permanent dwelling for Amaterasu. She finally received an oracle at Ise, where the goddess declared her love for the place. The Inner Shrine was established there, and the imperial house has maintained it ever since.

myths.title: The Twenty-Year Rebuilding
myths.text: The shikinen-zōtai tradition requires that the shrine buildings be reconstructed on adjacent plots every twenty years. The old structures are dismantled, and their timber is distributed to branch shrines. This cycle ensures that the architecture remains fresh and that the skills of sacred carpentry are passed down through generations.

myths.title: Okage-mairi
myths.text: In the Edo period, mass pilgrimages to Ise called okage-mairi swept the country. Villages would pool their resources and send representatives — sometimes whole communities — to walk the Ise-kaidō. These pilgrimages expressed popular devotion to Amaterasu and shaped the culture of travel in early modern Japan.

lore.syncretism: Ise has both resisted and absorbed outside influences. It remained the symbolic center of State Shinto in the modern period, yet its rituals and architecture preserve ancient Japanese forms. Buddhist influence was deliberately excluded from the Inner Shrine for long periods, making Ise a stronghold of 'pure' Shinto ideology — even as the broader Shinto tradition was itself shaped by Buddhist and continental models.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ise remains the most sacred destination in Shinto. The Ise-Shima region hosts the G7 summit's shrine visit; the rebuilding ceremonies draw national attention; and the phrase 'Ise ni ichido wa' ('to Ise at least once') still expresses a cultural aspiration. The simple, raised-floor architecture of Ise has influenced modern Japanese design and the global image of Shinto.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ise asks what it means to preserve by renewing. The shrine is never allowed to grow old; its decay is built into the plan. In a culture that often idolizes permanence, Ise teaches that sacred things must be remade, that craftsmanship is a form of prayer, and that the same place can be born again and again.

lore.archaeology: The Ise Grand Shrine complex includes the Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū), Outer Shrine (Gekū), and numerous auxiliary shrines. Archaeological investigations have clarified the shifting locations of successive rebuilding plots and the ancient use of the Isuzu River for ritual purification. The nearby Sengu Museum preserves building models and ritual implements from past rebuildings.
